items.title: Why Wendell Berry Didn’t Worry About the Future
items.description: Wendell Berry was not an easy man to reach. When I wanted to interview him for this magazine in the spring of 2015, his publicist warned me that a press request would take some doing. Berry didn’t have a cellphone. He didn’t use email. He didn’t even have a computer. He wrote most of his drafts by hand during the day, without electric light. And he definitely didn’t make himself available to any old reporter who wanted to talk. I knew this already, of course. Berry, who died on Monday at the age of 92, lived a life defined by acts of radical abstention. He said no emphatically and often; principled refusal was a central theme of his writing and the lore that surrounded him. The publicist spent the better part of a week trying to reach Berry on my behalf. This involved multiple phone calls to his farmhouse, in Henry County, Kentucky, where Berry and his wife, Tanya, had lived since the mid-1960s. Wendell spent most of his time outdoors, the publicist explained, so he often simply wasn’t around to hear the landline ring. After a while, though, she told me that she and Berry had managed to connect, and that he would consider my request. He asked that I write him a letter about the article I had in mind, which I emailed to the publicist so she could print it out and send it to him by post. [ From the February 1991 issue: Out of your car, off your horse ] A few weeks later, I received a voicemail from a number I didn’t recognize. “Hello, Mr. Fassler,” said a voice that was deep and hoarse with age. “This is Wendell Berry.” A giant of Luddism was speaking out of my iPhone. He asked me to call him back. When we spoke, he told me in a warm, genial way that I was out of luck. “I’m just so covered up with work,” he said, “and I can’t tell if it’s because I’m just busy or because I’m old.” But he’d thought a bit about my letter. I’d asked him to take part in “ By Heart ,” a series in which authors discussed the passages from literature that had most shaped their writing and outlook. He said that his forthcoming book, Our Only World , contained a section that the magazine might adapt in some way. It hinged on some verses from Jesus’s Sermon on the Mount, as described in the Gospel of Matthew: “Take no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.” He asked me to read that section of his book, and to call him back once I had so that we could talk. So I did. And I’ve been thinking about its message ever since. I was surprised, at first, that Berry felt so drawn to this specific moment from the Bible. Jesus’s instruction to not worry about the future seemed at odds with much of what Berry had written. Many of the social and environmental problems that Berry railed against were really problems of short-term thinking, including the pursuit of quick profit, the extractive poisoning of the land, and the love of cheap thrills over deeper, more hard-won pleasures. “Think not of tomorrow” seemed to better describe the ethos of Berry’s longtime nemeses: coal-industry strip miners, big agribusiness, the global financial system. It was also an odd choice for someone who seemed so concerned about the excesses of modern life. Berry struck me as someone who absolutely would fixate on the general worsening direction of things. Fretting about the future is a favorite preoccupation of the conscientious. Berry occasionally admitted to his own worried state of mind on the page, including in one of his best-known poem s : “When despair for the world grows in me,” he wrote, “I wake in the night at the least sound / in fear of what my life and my children’s lives may be.” Nevertheless, in the part of his book that he asked me to read, he wrote, “Taking thought for the morrow is, fairly predictably, a waste of time.” He insisted that what we call “the future” is a flimsy and insubstantial thing at best—a phantom we obsess over that never really arrives, or never arrives in the way we imagine. “Most of the bad possibilities I have worried about have never happened,” Berry wrote. “By taking thought for the morrow we have invested, and wasted, a lot of effort in preparing for morrows that never came.” Obsessing about the future, he argued, also has devastating moral consequences. It allows people to avoid engaging with the urgent realities of the present. I don’t know whether Berry, given his extremely offline lifestyle, ever learned about doomscrolling—the way social media can serve as a collective orgy of dread. But he’s right that, when people become too obsessed with a future that may or may not befall them, they tend to turn their back on the moment they’re in. “The time is coming when it will be too late to save the world. Oh, oh, oh,” he wrote, lampooning the handwringer in so many of us. “If that is the way our minds are afflicted, we and our world are dead already. The present is going by and we are not in it.” As I see it, this was the core purpose of Berry’s work: He dared his readers to live in a way that honors the situation at hand, at this very second. That mandate suffused everything he wrote about. He exhorted readers to enjoy the food on their plates, to bear witness to the places that surround them, and to revel in shared experience with the people in their orbit. Honoring the present was a joyful thing for Wendell Berry. It was also a form of rewarding but very difficult work. It meant slow, careful deliberation about the things he was willing to let into his life, whether that was a new piece of technology or a request from a journalist. And it meant searching for ways to disentangle himself, by turns and sometimes painfully, from destructive systems. The moral goal of a human being, he often argued, should be to do less harm right now. When one of his most famous essays, 1987’s “ Why I Am Not Going to Buy a Computer ,” resulted in astonished and outraged letters from readers, Berry replied by writing, “I did not say that I proposed to end forthwith all my involvement in harmful technology, for I do not know how to do that. I said merely that I want to limit such involvement, and to a certain extent I do know how to do that.” This response boils down to a simple, radical worldview: We must seek to understand the harms caused by the systems we’re implicated in, then strive to become less reliant on them. [ From the February 1992 issue: A jonquil for Mary Penn ] Berry was no purist. He understood that no 20th- or 21st-century American can live a wholly blameless life. He lamented needing to drive a truck, the unavoidable, occasional use of gas-powered equipment on his farm. He knew that his ancestors had enslaved their fellow human beings and that he, in direct and indirect ways, had benefited from that obscene bondage. “I am owned by the blood of all of them,” he wrote in an early poem, “My Great-Grandfather’s Slaves.” “We cannot be free of each other.” Moral blamelessness isn’t possible. But Berry’s larger point was that people should strive for something better, here and now. As he put it in Our Only World , with his trademark aphoristic brilliance: “Maybe we could give up saving the world and start to live savingly in it.” This reframes Jesus’s “sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof” as a simple, clarifying injunction: Forget the future, and work toward what is good today. I did speak with Berry a second time. We talked a little while about the Sermon on the Mount, but I didn’t get him to agree to a formal interview. I could tell he wanted to help me, to be a sport. Still, I sensed something else nagging at him: the irresistible presence of the now. He was here, living on this Earth. He had land to tend to, animals to care for, a wife to love, books to write—more than 50 of them, by the end. Maybe someday, in some dimly glimpsed future, he would find some more time to talk with me. But right then, at that moment, there was just too much to do.

items.title: Le mensonge a les jambes courtes, la vérité finira par éclater !
items.description: Le journaliste Mohamed Yousfi, rédacteur en chef du média d’investigation Alqatiba , arrêté et placé en garde-à-vue hier soir, vendredi 4 septembre 2026, a fait parvenir, par le biais de son avocate Hela Ben Salem, cette lettre à ses collègues journalistes et aux Tunisiens en général, pour les exhorter à défendre leur dignité et leurs droits. Nous traduisons cette lettre de l’arabe et la reproduisons ci-dessous… Mohamed Yousfi * Mon message aux journalistes indépendants de ce pays : N’ayez pas peur ; continuez à écrire, à vous exprimer, à porter la voix des citoyens, celle des personnes marginalisées et opprimées. Défendez l’État de droit, les droits humains et la dignité du citoyen tunisien — une dignité que nous avons perdue dans ce pays. Je m’adresse tout particulièrement à mes collègues d’Alqatiba : Poursuivez le chemin que nous avons tracé ; n’ayez crainte ; j’ai une immense confiance en vous. Les tentatives de harcèlement et d’acharnement dont je fais l’objet ne visent en réalité qu’à atteindre Alqatiba et à entraver la ligne éditoriale indépendante de cette entreprise. Tous les Tunisiens connaissent la valeur de cette plateforme, ainsi que ses réalisations et sa contribution au droit d’accès à l’information et au journalisme d’investigation. Aujourd’hui, les faits, enquêtes et données présentés par Alqatiba sont utilisés par la justice elle-même comme référence dans des affaires majeures d’évasion fiscale, de blanchiment d’argent et de corruption ; c'est l’un des derniers bastions de la liberté de pensée, d’expression et de la presse. Ce n’est pas Mohamed Yousfi qui est sanctionné aujourd’hui, mais Alqatiba, pour son attachement à son indépendance et aux valeurs journalistiques léguées par la Révolution, au prix du sang des martyrs et des blessés. Il est donc impératif de poursuivre ce chemin, et j’ai une confiance totale en mes collègues d’Alqatiba. Mon message aux Tunisiens : si je suis actuellement en garde à vue, c’est pour une raison très simple : j’exerce mon métier de journaliste de manière indépendante et professionnelle. Je défends votre droit à une vie digne, à l’eau, à l’électricité, à la santé et à l’enseignement public, ainsi que votre droit de défendre votre dignité, de bénéficier d’une presse libre et d’accéder à l’information. Les véritables criminels sont ces blogueurs corrompus qui tentent de salir la réputation des journalistes libres du pays ; mais le mensonge a les jambes courtes. Aujourd’hui, j’ai été enlevé alors que j’exerçais mes fonctions de journaliste. On m’a appréhendé comme si j’avais été pris en flagrant délit ou que je tentais de fuir, alors qu’il aurait suffi de me convoquer : mon identité et mon adresse sont connues, et il n’y avait aucune raison de faire une telle démonstration de force. Tenter de me discréditer en m’accusant de blanchiment d’argent relève de l’absurde et témoigne de la faillite de ce système. Au moment de mon arrestation, je ne possédais rien : ni argent, ni biens immobiliers. Je vis de mon salaire et mon compte bancaire est même débiteur de quelques dinars. Espérons que cette épreuve passera ; la vérité finira par éclater, tôt ou tard. Traduit de l'arabe. * Journaliste, rédacteur en chef d'Alqatiba. items.title: Putin orders three-day halt to strikes on Kyiv for US envoys' visit
items.description: Russian President Vladimir Putin has ordered a three-day halt to strikes against Kyiv, a move linked to preparations for contacts with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Saturday. "The meeting with President Putin will indeed take place, and there will be talks. As a rule, such meetings have been quite lengthy in the past. Let us wait and see. We will certainly keep you informed," Peskov told journalists. Peskov also urged against making predictions about settlement proposals and called for waiting for the outcome of Putin's meeting with the US negotiators. Witkoff and Kushner landed at Moscow's Vnukovo Airport at 12:52 p.m. local time (0952 GMT) on Saturday. They were welcomed at the airport by Russia's special presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev. Peskov's statement came hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said earlier in the day that Russia had struck airports in Kyiv and its southeastern suburb of Boryspil overnight. "Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the U.S. side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine and land at Kyiv Airport or Boryspil Airport," Zelenskyy said in a post on X. Zelenskyy said that Ukraine had taken note of the Russian move and would adjust its operations next week accordingly with regard to Russian airspace. Zelenskyy also said on Thursday that he expected to meet Trump's envoys in the Ukrainian capital in the coming days.

items.title: Super-strong El Nino projected to persist into summer 2027
items.description: China’s National Climate Center (NCC) said this week that a super-strong El Nino event is taking shape in the tropical Pacific, with its impacts potentially extending into the summer of 2027. The NCC expects sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific to continue rising amid fluctuations, peaking around November and December. The peak intensity is projected to exceed 2.5 degrees Celsius, indicating a super-strong event. Chen Lijuan, the NCC’s chief forecaster, said the event could surpass the three previous super-strong El Nino events recorded in 1982/1983, 1997/1998 and 2015/2016, potentially making it the strongest since records began. Gu Wei, also a chief forecaster at the NCC, said China is likely to experience significant climate anomalies in the coming seasons as El Nino develops rapidly. Gu said its influence may already be evident in this summer’s weather, with central and eastern China generally facing heightened flood risks. Looking ahead, Gu said El Nino is expected to have a greater impact on China’s temperatures and precipitation through the autumn and winter. She forecast above-average winter precipitation across much of southern China, while overall temperatures are expected to be warmer than usual. However, frequent incursions of cold air could still produce sharp swings between warm and cold conditions. Gu also warned that El Nino’s impact on China’s climate could become even more pronounced in the summer of 2027. Precipitation is expected to be generally above normal across central and eastern China, with particularly high risks of torrential rain and flooding along the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River. The NCC also stressed that the intensity of an El Nino event alone does not determine how severe its impacts will be in any particular location.

items.title: China steps up monitoring of risk areas in mudslide-hit Gyirong
items.description: More than 2,300 rescuers, including 726 personnel from the Chinese People's Liberation Army and the People's Armed Police Force, have joined search and rescue operations at mudslide-hit Gyirong Port in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region. The mudslide, triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal on August 26, has left 31 people dead and 531 others missing in Xizang as of Saturday, according to the local emergency response and rescue command center. So far, more than 400 vehicles, more than 8,000 sets of rescue equipment and over 800 drones have been deployed for deeper search operations. In addition, charitable donations for relief efforts following the massive mudslide have exceeded 660 million yuan (about $98.34 million), according to China's Ministry of Civil Affairs. Authorities have inspected and monitored 112 potential hazard sites, identifying a total of 58 geological hazard sites, including 7 high-risk areas. Drones have been deployed to cover 65 square kilometers of the affected area, while over 40 warning signs have been installed at medium-risk and high-risk locations. Additionally, dynamic checks and inspections are being carried out along the rescue routes to ensure ongoing safety. Normal water flow of previous barrier lake, 14 glacial lakes remain stable Official aerial surveys show a level of normal water flow in the upstream and downstream river channels of a previous barrier lake. The lake formed near the confluence of the Chhochen Khola River in Nepal and Purepu Zangbo River in China. Authorities say 14 glacial lakes also remain generally stable. Meteorological data shows that light to moderate rain is expected around Gyirong Port in the coming days. Slope radar deployed in hard-hit core area A slope radar system has been deployed in the core disaster-hit area of Gyirong Port to monitor secondary geological hazards. The radar equipment, capable of detecting millimeter-level ground displacements, is being used to monitor mountain slopes for potential landslides and collapses around the clock. According to the Ministry of Emergency Management, the National Work Safety Emergency Rescue Survey Team, together with two national tunnel rescue teams, has formed a joint monitoring group to operate the radar units in the core zone. The systems provide real-time data to on-site rescue commanders, enabling early warnings and timely evacuation in the event of imminent slope failures. Support for Nepal Nepali Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said China has provided Nepal with near-real-time information to help authorities stay alert for potential future disasters. He expressed deep gratitude for China's "very proactive support," which has included emergency cash, three batches of relief supplies, and the dispatch of tunnel rescue and DNA identification experts. The Nepali foreign minister noted that rescue operations remain extremely difficult as roads and bridges in the affected region are severely damaged, leaving some areas inaccessible by land. He added that hundreds of Nepali citizens on the Chinese side of the border have been properly accommodated by the Chinese authorities. Khanal called for stronger Nepal-China cooperation in studying and preserving the Himalayan ecosystem, emphasizing that "the Himalayan ecosystem is our shared future," and urging joint efforts to address climate change challenges. items.title: Burkina Faso : La pédiatrie du CHR de Koudougou dotée d’un nouveau bâtiment grâce à la coopération chinoise
items.description: Le service de pédiatrie du Centre hospitalier régional (CHR) de Koudougou renforce ses capacités d’accueil. Un nouveau bâtiment de 20 lits, réalisé avec l’appui de la Chine, a été officiellement remis à l’établissement ce 4 septembre 2026. Une infrastructure qui arrive à point nommé au regard de la forte pression exercée sur les capacités d’hospitalisation. Désormais, les enfants hospitalisés au CHR de Koudougou disposent de 20 lits supplémentaires. Le nouveau bâtiment a été officiellement remis à l’établissement au cours d’une cérémonie ponctuée par la remise des clés, la signature du procès-verbal, la coupure du ruban symbolique et la visite des chambres. Cette extension porte la capacité globale du CHR de Koudougou de 299 à 319 lits, une augmentation qui devrait permettre de mieux répondre à la demande, particulièrement forte dans le service de pédiatrie. Et pour cause : au cours des sept premiers mois de 2026, le taux d’occupation des lits du CHR a atteint 155,05 %, alors que la norme maximale est fixée à 80 %, selon la directrice générale de l’établissement, Habibou Ouédraogo. « Deux enfants sur un même lit » Derrière ces chiffres se cache une réalité parfois difficile pour les soignants, les enfants malades et leurs accompagnants. Le chef du service de pédiatrie, le médecin-pédiatre Salif Kiendrebéogo, témoigne des difficultés rencontrées lors des périodes de forte affluence. « Certaines périodes de l’année sont particulièrement difficiles en raison de affluence », explique-t-il. Le manque de lits a des conséquences particulièrement préoccupantes. « Le manque de lits obligeait parfois le personnel à installer deux enfants sur un même lit », poursuit le médecin. Une situation qui compliquait non seulement l’organisation des soins, mais aussi le séjour des jeunes patients et de leurs accompagnants. Avec ces 20 nouveaux lits, l’espoir est donc de voir cette pression diminuer et les conditions de prise en charge s’améliorer. Plus de 40 millions de francs CFA mobilisés La réalisation de cette infrastructure a été rendue possible grâce à l’appui de l’ambassade de la République populaire de Chine au Burkina Faso. La construction du bâtiment a coûté 32 millions de francs CFA, auxquels s’ajoutent 8 millions de francs CFA de matériel médico-technique, soit une contribution globale de plus de 40 millions de francs CFA. Représentant l’ambassadeur de Chine au Burkina Faso, Zhao Deyong, la ministre conseillère, Li Qi, a réaffirmé la volonté de son pays de poursuivre son accompagnement dans le domaine sanitaire. Elle a notamment rappelé que « 2026 marque le 50e anniversaire de l’envoi de la première mission médicale chinoise au Burkina Faso » . La coopération sanitaire entre les deux pays devrait d’ailleurs se poursuivre. Li Qi a annoncé « un nouvel appui de plus de 40 millions de francs CFA destiné à l’extension de la pédiatrie et à l’acquisition de matériel médical ». « Un cadre plus confortable » pour les enfants La réalisation a également été saluée par la délégation spéciale communale de Koudougou. Représentant son président, Odette Bassié a souligné l’importance de cette infrastructure dans l’amélioration de l’offre de soins et de la prise en charge des enfants. Du côté des jeunes bénéficiaires, le sentiment est également positif. Représentante des enfants, Merveille Simporé estime que ce nouvel espace permettra aux patients d’être accueillis et soignés dans « un cadre plus confortable » . La cérémonie a par ailleurs été l’occasion de rendre hommage à huit médecins chinois décédés dans les années 1980 alors qu’ils étaient en mission au Burkina Faso. La délégation chinoise s’est recueillie sur leurs tombes au cimetière municipal de Koudougou. Au-delà des murs et des nouveaux lits, ce bâtiment de pédiatrie traduit ainsi une volonté de renforcer les capacités du CHR de Koudougou face à l’affluence. Pour les enfants et leurs familles, il porte surtout la promesse d’une prise en charge dans des conditions plus adaptées. items.title: Corinne Lepage, une vie consacrée à la défense de l’environnement
items.description: C’est la rentrée de l’émission “Avec Judith”. Pour ce premier épisode, Judith reçoit Corinne Lepage, ancienne ministre de l’Environnement, avocate et pionnière du droit environnemental. Elle revient sur cinquante ans de combats pour l’environnement et sur l’état de l’écologie aujourd’hui. Au fil de l’entretien, Corinne Lepage revient également sur les grands procès qui ont contribué à construire le droit de l’environnement, de l’Erika à la justice climatique, mais aussi sur le nucléaire, les énergies renouvelables, la santé publique, la place des femmes et la défense de l’État de droit.

items.title: J. D. Vance’s Disingenuous Defense of Tucker Carlson
items.description: When J. D. Vance was asked at a press conference on Thursday about his relationship with Tucker Carlson, the media personality and ultra-right-wing conspiracy theorist, he displayed a surprising side of himself: human, vulnerable, almost touchingly naive. “Tucker is a friend, despite the fact that we disagree on a number of things,” the vice president said. “And I’m not going to play the game where I throw friends under the bus because I have political disagreements with them. I think that is a terrible place for the United States to go. And if you have a disagreement with somebody politically, even over a deeply held issue, you should still be friends with that person, because the whole republic depends on people of different perspectives being able to talk to one another.” This was a matter not of politics, Vance was at pains to emphasize, but of friendship . If Vance were to renounce Carlson over a matter as trivial as, say, Carlson’s oddly positive assessment of Adolf Hitler, what hope is there for society? The bonds of affection between Vance and Carlson are the very glue holding together the American experiment. And yet, tempting though it might be to imagine Vance clasping hands with the children of the world and teaching them to sing in perfect harmony, some notes of skepticism are warranted. Perhaps Vance’s affection for Carlson has more to do with holding the loyalty of his friend’s enormous audience. [ Peter Wehner: What J. D. Vance once knew ] For one, Vance is not known for cordially disagreeing with people. He has accumulated an unusual number of bitter enemies by flinging insults at people—including Senate Democrats (“You’re full of shit, and everyone knows it”), reporters (“scumbags”), and “childless cat ladies.” Last month, Vance hurled himself into an obscure debate over burrito prices to make a gratuitous swipe at a conservative Washington Post columnist’s weight. At the very same press conference where he waxed so earnestly about open dialogue, Vance mocked the idea that he would talk to former President Biden at the 9/11 ceremony (“I’m really looking forward to hanging out with Joe Biden. I’m sure that we’ll have many, many intense intellectual conversations, and it’ll be great”) and dismissed the Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed as “a crazy person.” Vance’s dig at El-Sayed, and the context in which he made it, revealed a lot more about his reasons for maintaining the alliance with Carlson than did his encomium to friendship. Vance was trying to illustrate that he and Carlson do not agree on everything. Carlson had recently praised El-Sayed as “America First” and “literally Trumpian,” apparently calculating that the candidate’s anti-Zionism outweighs his many left-wing positions. That view was the one Vance chose to highlight as his point of disagreement, rather than several other controversial remarks Carlson has made. Examples include but are not limited to his endorsement of “Great Replacement” and other conspiracy theories, his expressions of sympathy for Russia and its war against Ukraine, and his sympathetic interviews with figures such as Nick Fuentes, Alex Jones, and the World War II–revisionist historian Darryl Cooper, who called Winston Churchill “the chief villain of the Second World War” and described much of the Holocaust as mistaken deaths resulting from poor planning. All of these statements have left Carlson teetering at the edge of respectability within the Republican Party. He has become one of the most prominent exponents of a strain of right-wing populism that flirts with and in some cases embraces isolationism, anti-Semitism, and general crackpottery. Vance has courted this faction of the right. He and Carlson have a partnership that has lasted nearly a decade and has yielded dozens of interviews. In the course of this partnership, they may well have formed a genuine friendship. But Vance has discarded plenty of friends as he has cycled through various political identities. The difference between Vance’s ex-friends and Carlson is that Carlson is still a useful ally in a Republican factional conflict. When Carlson upset Fox News in 2021 by endorsing the Great Replacement theory, which holds that Democrats are using illegal immigration to replace the current electorate and cement power, Vance wrote on social media , “Tucker Carlson is the only powerful figure who consistently challenges elite dogma—on both cultural and economic questions. That is why they try to destroy him. Don’t fall for it this time, or any other.” Vance went on to endorse the same theory in advance of the next midterm elections. “Democrat politicians who have decided that they can’t win reelection in 2022 unless they bring in a large number of new voters to replace the voters that are already here” are orchestrating lax border enforcement, he said on Carlson’s show that year. The Carlson-Vance partnership has generated more conservative blowback over the past few years as Carlson has progressed from skepticism of Israel into anti-Semitism , which Carlson denies . Traditional Republicans who have supported, or at least gone along with, the party’s attacks on Muslims and immigrants and its rejection of democratic norms have spoken out against cracking the door open for anti-Semites. Building an authoritarian, ultranationalist party that marinates in populist conspiracy theories but that abhors anti-Semitism turns out to be tricky. [ Helen Lewis: Carlson and Vance—two smart guys who play dumb for power ] Vance, heading into his expected 2028 presidential campaign, has a strong incentive to try to harness this right-wing energy. His political interests would be served if Republicans were to stop attacking Carlson and if Carlson were to tone down his criticism of the GOP. Hence, he seemed less concerned that Carlson had crossed a moral line than that, in the Michigan Senate race, he had crossed party lines. Carlson praising a member of the Democratic Party is more threatening to Vance than Carlson praising an apologist for the National Socialist German Workers’ Party. At this week’s press conference, the reporter asked Vance, “What do you say to those who are uneasy with your close relationship with Carlson and claim that you’re avoiding addressing a lot of these issues, which may be causing divisions within the GOP?” “What a travesty it is that in the United States of America, we let political disagreements define who our friends are going to be and not going to be,” Vance said. “So, yeah, Tucker is a friend of mine.” Suppose Carlson decided to support someone other than Vance for president in 2028. Does anybody think their friendship would survive?

items.title: The Rush-Job Presidency
items.description: Construction is notoriously slow-going work. But in Donald Trump’s Washington, cranes and bulldozers appear like DoorDash deliveries: fast, frictionless, and on demand. To build the president’s White House ballroom, roughly 250 workers have been pouring concrete and installing steel framework, keeping the site humming for 20 hours a day, seven days a week. The National Park Service has proposed a similarly intensive schedule for Trump’s planned triumphal arch: Construction will begin, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum announced on Thursday, in the next two weeks. And officials are trying to shut down the Kennedy Center for two years to carry out renovations that consultants say will take twice as long if the building remains open during the work. These are very different and ambitious projects, but they share the same presumed deadline: January 20, 2029. They also share a risk: The compressed schedules could lead to shoddy work that will require more repairs later. Trump has less than three years to complete his transformation of Washington, D.C., before his projects fall into—and perhaps die in—the hands of a successor. “Nobody will do it once I’m gone. When I leave here, nobody will,” he told New York magazine. The next president, whomever they are, likely won’t share Trump’s enthusiasm for gold finishes and Italian marble. To get the work done, his administration has found ways to circumvent the procedural obstacles that tend to slow federal projects. Construction—one of the world’s least productive industries—may present its own paradox. Research has shown that long hours, additional shifts, and overlapping work tasks can shorten a project’s timeline—but only to a point. In many cases, the effort to build faster can invite new delays, higher costs, and revisions. Trump’s botched repairs to the Reflecting Pool ahead of the nation’s 250th-birthday celebrations, in July, offer a classic example of the problem. The ballroom project, a hulking party venue that overshadows the White House’s main building and its modest neoclassical design, could be another. The Supreme Court ruled 5–4 this week that its construction could continue, saying that the preservationists trying to halt the project did not have standing to sue. The three liberal dissenting justices—along with, notably, Chief Justice John G. Roberts—argued that the construction was “likely unlawful.” But government filings claim that it’s already 65 percent complete—even as project leaders have continually revised design plans. By the time a new lawsuit from a challenger with stronger standing advances through the courts, how far along will the ballroom be? [ Read: The Court’s ballroom decision is a sign of deeper problems ] “We have hundreds of happy construction workers in D.C. busily doing their job building the finest Ballroom/Military complex anywhere in the World,” Trump wrote on Truth Social this week after the Supreme Court decision. With his lawyers saying that the project will be “substantially” finished by November, the clock is ticking fast. Trump’s building spree presents a tricky calculation: The returns he wants are about time rather than cost. But speed in construction can get expensive fast, especially for a project whose anticipated costs have been hard to nail down. When Trump announced the ballroom plans in July 2025, he put the price at roughly $200 million, to be paid for by private donors. By October, he’d knocked down the East Wing of the White House without seeking any approvals. As the work has started, stopped (because of the preservationists’ lawsuit), and started again, the original estimate has tripled to $600 million, and taxpayers are expected to cover half of that amount, according to internal documents from the ballroom’s general contractor, Clark Construction, that were obtained by The Washington Post . Those projections could rise again. “Accelerated construction is always at higher cost, no matter what you do,” Awad Hanna, the chair of the construction-engineering and -management program at the University of Wisconsin at Madison, told me. There are essentially three ways to make construction move faster, according to Hanna: Workers can put in overtime, contractors can add second or third shifts, or the project can resort to overmanning—that is, adding an unusually large number of workers to a site. Each method may buy some time but sacrifices some productivity, Hanna said. Researchers have documented that trade-off for decades. A 1997 study published by the American Society of Civil Engineers examined 121 weeks of labor-productivity data from four industrial projects and found efficiency losses of roughly 10 to 15 percent for 50-to-60-hour workweeks. Hanna’s own research has found similar patterns. With overmanning, the problem is that there’s only so much room for specific tasks to be performed. As the site fills up with workers, they can find themselves competing for tools, materials, and information—or simply getting in one another’s way. Meanwhile, overtime can lead to fatigue for workers who are spending 10 to 12 hours on their feet, carrying heavy objects while also needing to remain diligent about their own safety. There is another way to speed up construction without adding hours or workers: starting construction before a design is complete. The industry calls this fast-tracking. But a 2023 study found that construction professionals perceived the fast-track strategy as posing a different set of risks, including construction errors and productivity declines, when better productivity is supposed to be the whole point. A certain amount of secrecy surrounds the White House worksite, in part because of a large military structure that is being built underground, beneath where the ballroom will stand. The methods to speed up the work are unclear, although the teams behind the project are reputable: Clark Construction is a seasoned federal contractor, and the architectural firm Shalom Baranes Associates repaired the Pentagon after 9/11. A White House spokesperson told me that the project is proceeding with the 20-hour schedule for now. In April, Trump turned his focus to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a century-old landmark that has long struggled with leaks and algae blooms. Trump first claimed that he could complete a repair project in a week for less than $2 million. “I have a guy who’s unbelievable at doing swimming pools,” he told reporters at the time. The costs climbed to more than $16 million, which included the installation of a waterproof liner tinted in a color that he called American-flag blue. But shortly after the pool reopened, in June, algae returned in force and the sealant peeled, leading crews to repeatedly drain and scrub the basin over the summer. Now it sits completely empty and fenced off. Trump accused vandals of damaging the pool, but his own U.S. attorney for D.C. refuted those claims, pointing to the contractor’s failures and the Interior Department providing “less than fulsome information at the outset of the case.” Federal officials recently hired a new contractor to deal with the algae. Trump has already cleared one obstacle blocking the ballroom. But the legal case is not over. Following the emergency ruling, the government still has to formally ask the Supreme Court to hear its appeal. And the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which brought the suit against Trump, can continue a fight in the lower courts. For each of Trump’s Washington projects, officials have beefed up their justifications in one way or another in the face of legal challenges. In the administration’s view: The Kennedy Center may have to be “taken down” if its planned two-year shutdown for renovations is blocked. (Critics have pushed back on officials’ claims that the building’s conditions are existentially dire.) The Reflecting Pool’s needed repairs were urgent enough to exempt them from the typical competitive-bidding process. (The urgency was the July 4 celebrations.) And now? The White House ballroom is needed for security reasons, because it’s connected to a military bunker. [ Read: The Kennedy Center has a problem that courts can’t fix ] The administration has also pointed to the ballroom’s progress in arguing against an injunction, raising a larger question about whether speed itself has become a form of power in Trump’s building spree. If a president can build faster than Congress or regulators can review, legal constraints may matter less in practice—not because they have disappeared but because enforcing them comes too late. This week’s Supreme Court ruling has already prompted at least one federal judge to consider its implications for another Trump project. Yesterday, U.S. District Judge Carl J. Nichols ordered lawyers representing the Interior Department to address how the Court’s ballroom decision affects its pending motion to dismiss a lawsuit challenging work on the Reflecting Pool. When asked about the start of excavations for the triumphal arch, the White House spokesperson said in an email, “Work will begin that does not require approval, but rather helps in the process. We will of course continue on our path of seeking final approval from all applicable entities.” The arch still needs final approval from the National Capital Planning Commission, to which Trump has added loyalists. But the administration has also been working to water down historic-preservation rules governing federal projects just as the arch has become subject to that process. Meanwhile, the Kennedy Center—which Trump also controls—cannot start its renovation until a judge signs off on the latest plan. But this week, the center removed a prominent artwork near the Potomac River, a sign that top-down change has begun. All three projects—the ballroom, the arch, and the Kennedy Center—may soon be moving forward simultaneously, red tape cleared (or ignored). But sped-up construction can impose its own obstacles. When unexpected delays crop up, even presidents have to wait.

items.title: Why I Want More AI at Dartmouth
items.description: Students returning to campus this semester are arriving with a great deal of anxiety about AI and what it will mean for their lives after college. They are right to be worried. New research from Stanford shows that, even though the much-hyped AI job apocalypse has yet to materialize, the technology has already caused a nearly 20 percent drop in employment for young workers in AI-exposed occupations, such as computer programming and customer-service work. Anxiety over the looming threat of AI may seem novel, but as a cognitive scientist who has long studied how fear affects learning and performance, I am all too familiar with this kind of unease. This is how I know it is also curable. Several years ago, my former graduate student Ian Lyons and I invited people who were anxious about math to have their brains scanned while they took a math test. We were surprised to find that it wasn’t the test itself that sent people’s brains into a panic. Rather, the neural signals associated with threat detection and pain were most acute when people were merely anticipating the test. [ John Paul Rollert: A society of cheats ] We are all now living through AI’s waiting-for-the-math-test phase. AI is transforming classrooms, workplaces, and hiring needs—and experts say more turbulence is coming. Teachers and students are struggling to parse the difference between deploying AI effectively and exploiting the technology to cheat. But rather than tackling this disruptive change and the resulting anxiety head-on, many educators are trying to make AI simply go away. The University of Chicago’s social-science faculty have prohibited most technology and banned the use of AI tools from their core classes. Although law firms are beginning to embrace the benefits of generative AI, the technology apparently makes many law schools squeamish. In May, the UC Berkeley School of Law announced that students are prohibited from using AI in “conceptualizing, outlining, drafting, revising, translating, or editing any work submitted for credit.” The University of Chicago Law School has decided to ban all screens from first-year classrooms entirely. In an atmosphere of uncertainty—and given prevailing concerns about students using AI to cheat—such bans would seem to make some sense. But draconian mandates and screenless classes can’t be the only ways that colleges deal with AI. If universities hope to remain relevant in a world shaped by artificial intelligence, they should strive to guide students to understand and use these tools productively. In my research of math anxiety, we found that the best cure was practicing math. This points to a way forward. When we supply students with the space to thoughtfully explore and engage with these tools, we can help ensure that they graduate into an AI-enabled workforce with more confidence and competence than fear, and with an appreciation for how to use AI tools ethically. But if higher education opts for prohibition over practice, we will squander the chance to help shape how this technology gets used in the world—ensuring that the private sector will do this for us instead. Colleges must start by being clear about what a degree is actually worth in the AI age. At Dartmouth, the Ivy League university where I am president, we believe it’s our job to teach students how to do what AI can’t: decide which questions to ask, exercise sound judgment, navigate ethical complexity, reckon with uncertainty, and take responsibility for their decisions. Then, we have to give them the chance to practice these skills in concert with AI. Harnessing AI ethically and productively requires understanding what the technology is and where it falls short. This is why Dartmouth, along with other schools such as Johns Hopkins University and Rollins College, has employed a critical AI librarian , an educator who helps students and faculty interrogate these models, recognize their biases, and spot unsupported claims. At our DALI Lab , where students design and create technological products, they can now build and stress-test their own AI models, which elevates their understanding of the risks and rewards at play. Our ambition at Dartmouth is for every undergraduate to experience a team-based AI project that relates to their coursework by the time they graduate. Practice using AI matters even more when students start to specialize. To help prepare business students for AI use in the real world, Dartmouth’s Tuck School of Business now requires that they use the technology to build and test solutions for clients in their First-Year Project. Thanks to this experience, students who lacked AI expertise when they entered the program reported greater confidence using the technology by the end of their first year. At Dartmouth’s Geisel School of Medicine, our faculty developed an AI Patient Actor to help medical-school students sharpen their communication and interpersonal skills with the benefit of real-time feedback. The tool is now being used by more than 100 medical institutions worldwide. [ Walt Hunter: Bring back the blue-book exam ] Adapting the college experience for the AI era will be an ongoing process, and there is much work to do. But these examples demonstrate what’s both possible and necessary in higher education. Our job as educators is to teach students how to approach AI critically, help them see what AI can’t answer, and practice using these tools effectively. When these students graduate and are out in the world, employers will certainly expect that they have these skills already. Globally, jobs that require advanced AI skills are growing eight times faster than the job market overall, according to an analysis from the professional-services network PwC. At the same time, entry-level roles in AI-exposed fields are more than seven times likelier than other entry-level jobs to require the human skills once reserved for senior executives, including discernment, creativity, and leadership. Never before has the ability to harmonize critical thinking and technology mattered more for graduates. There will not—and should not—be a one-size-fits-all solution to the challenges of supplying this education. One professor may decide that students should write their essays in a blue book in class, while another may ask them to use an AI tool and audit every step of this work. Both choices will serve students when faculty are clear about their ambitions and standards. But outright bans or vague curbs afford no opportunities for students to better understand how to work ethically and effectively with AI. Seventy years ago, pioneering computer scientists launched the field of artificial intelligence on Dartmouth’s campus. That history gives our institution some responsibility for what comes next —not just to prepare students for a future defined by AI, but to give them the tools to help shape that future themselves. If colleges and universities sit out this revolution, we abdicate a sacred commitment that has guided American higher education for centuries: to prepare the next generation of leaders to navigate an ever-changing, always complicated, and frequently perilous world. In a world that promises to be defined by AI, universities that fail to produce graduates who can use it productively will consign themselves to irrelevance.

items.title: Manifestations Gen Z à Madagascar : l'ex-président du Sénat condamné à dix ans de prison
items.description: À Madagascar, la justice frappe l'un des visages les plus redoutés de l'ancien régime. L'ex-président du Sénat, le général Richard Ravalomanana, a été condamné à dix ans de travaux forcés pour son rôle dans la répression sanglante des manifestations de la Gen Z, en septembre et octobre 2025.
